descriptionChirho: To bring an action, discourse, or period of time to its conclusion; to finish doing something, used in the active voice with a transitive object. This is the primary active sense of τελέω, covering Jesus finishing his discourses in Matthew (7:28, 11:1, 13:53, 19:1, 26:1 ἐτέλεσεν), completing appointed tasks (Lk 2:39 ἐτέλεσαν, Acts 13:29 ἐτέλεσαν), Paul finishing his race (2 Tim 4:7 τετέλεκα), finishing cities of Israel (Mt 10:23), and the two witnesses finishing their testimony (Rev 11:7). Glosses converge: Arabic أَكمَلَ, German vollendet, Hebrew סִיֵּם/כִּלָּה, Korean 마치다, Spanish terminó/completaron.

To be brought to completion or fulfillment, used in the passive or middle voice of divine purposes, prophecies, appointed times, and eschatological events reaching their destined conclusion. This covers Jesus' cry Τετέλεσται (Jn 19:30, 'It is finished'), prophetic fulfillment (Lk 12:50, 18:31, 22:37), the perfecting of divine power in weakness (2 Cor 12:9), the completion of God's wrath (Rev 10:7, 15:1,8), the fulfillment of God's purposes (Rev 17:17, 20:3,5,7). Glosses point to passive accomplishment: Arabic قَدْ اكْتَمَلَ/تَتِمَّ, Hebrew נִשְׁלַם/יִכְלוּ, Korean 완성되었다/이루어지다, Spanish consumado/cumplidas/terminados.

To fulfill, carry out, or keep a law, commandment, or moral obligation, with a connotation of obedient performance or observance. In Rom 2:27, the physically uncircumcised person who keeps the law (τελοῦσα τὸν νόμον); in Gal 5:16, not fulfilling the desire of the flesh (τελέσητε); in Jas 2:8, fulfilling the royal law (τελεῖτε νόμον βασιλικόν). The glosses emphasize fulfillment-as-obedience: Arabic المُكمِلَةُ, Hebrew מְמַלֵּאָה/תְמַלְּאוּ/תְּקַיְּמוּ (fulfill/carry out), Korean 이행하다/이루다 (perform/fulfill), Spanish que cumple/cumpláis/cumplís.

To pay taxes, tribute, or a financial obligation, a specialized commercial sense of τελέω meaning to settle what is owed. In Mt 17:24, the question about whether Jesus pays the temple tax (τελεῖ τὰ δίδραχμα), and in Rom 13:6, the reason believers pay taxes (φόρους τελεῖτε). The glosses distinctively reflect financial payment rather than general completion: Arabic يَدْفَعُ/تَدْفَعُونَ (pay), Hebrew מְשַׁלֵּם/מְשַׁלְּמִים (pay), Korean 내다/내느니 (pay out), Spanish paga/pagáis. This sense is well attested in classical Greek for discharging financial obligations.
